# Assignment 2

### Load tidyverse

```{R}
library(tidyverse)
```

### Load and save Wastes.csv and Year_State_ID.csv

```{R}
waste <- read_csv("data/Wastes.csv")
waste

year_state_id <- read_csv("data/Year_State_ID.csv")
year_state_id
```

## Determining how to handling missing value

Prior to conducting analysis, I will handle missing values by first observing how many entries will be cleared off if I simply drop all missing value.

```{R}
missing_entries <- waste %>% 
  filter(if_any(everything(), is.na))
missing_entries 
```

The NA values observed:

1. A row of Category = "Space debris" has several NA values across Case_ID, Year_State_ID, Stream, Fate, Tonnes, Core_Non-core and Description. Hence, the suitable approach is to drop this case.

```{R}
waste_drop <- waste %>%
  filter(is.na(Category) | Category != "Space debris")

waste_drop %>% 
  filter(if_any(everything(), is.na))
```

2. The rest only has one variable with NA value. The NAs are small in number and located in few cases and variables. Hence, the suitable approach is to impute these values by replacing with appropriate values by doing analysis and observation as we move on to each task.

## Q1. Number of unique "Category" values in Wastes.csv

Observe unique category

```{R}
waste_drop %>%
  select(Category) %>%
  distinct(Category)
```

Some concerning Category are observed. We need to make the Category naming consistent and reassign an appropriate value for misassigned Category.

```{R}
# record a list of concerning values 
concerning_category <- c(
  "Building & demolition materials",
  "Toxic wastes",
  "Plastic",
  "organics",
  "Aluminium",
  "Metals & Organics",
  "Toxic wastes",
  "Recycling"
) 

# inspect concerning Category values to determine appropriate way on how to replace
waste_drop %>%
  filter(
    Category %in% concerning_category |
      is.na(Category)
  ) %>%
  select(
    Category,
    Type,
    Stream,
    Fate
  )
```

Some concerning Category are observed: 
1. "Building & demolition materials" and "Building and demolition materials" is the same Category but naming unconsistency. 
2. "Hazardous wastes" and "HW" is the same Category but naming unconsistency. 
3. "Plastic" and "Plastics" is the same Category but naming unconsistency. 4. "organics" and "Organics" is the same Category but naming unconsistency. 
5. "Aluminium" is a Type, not Category. Should be replaced with "Metals" 6. "Metals & Organics" entry has Type of "Food organics". Should be replaced with Category of "Organics". 
7. "Toxic wastes" has Type mentioning "hazardous wastes". Should be replaced with "Hazardous wastes" for consistency. 
8. "Recycling" entry has Type "Polyvinyl chloride (PVC) (3)", which reflects a Category "Plastics". Furthermore, "Recycling" is a Fate, not a Category.

Some concerning NA Category are further analyse to determine a suitable replacement. We can create a na_category_type table to infer waste of similar Type has what kind of category.
This is done by joining na_category_type and waste_drop table.
```{R}
na_category_type <- waste_drop %>% 
  filter(
    is.na(Category)
  ) %>% distinct(Type)

na_category_type

waste %>% semi_join(
  na_category_type,
  by = "Type"
) %>% select(Category, Type)
```
It is observed that the NA Category values with Type of "Other soil/sludges (other N)" and "Paints, resins, inks, organic sludges (F)" belongs to Category of "Hazardous wastes", informing us:
9. NA entry with Type of "Other soil/sludges (other N)" and "Paints, resins, inks, organic sludges (F)", which is suitable to be replaced with "Hazardous wastes".

Now, values of Category column will be updated using recode() and case_when() accordingly.

```{R}
# replace for consistency and correctness
waste_unique <- waste_drop %>%
  filter(!is.na(Category)) %>%
  mutate(
    Category = recode(
      Category,
      # naming consistency
      "HW" = "Hazardous wastes",
      "Plastic" = "Plastics",
      "organics" = "Organics",
      "Building and demolition materials" = "Building & demolition materials",
      
      # miscategorisation
      "Aluminium" = "Metals",
      "Metals & Organics" = "Organics",
      "Toxic wastes" = "Hazardous wastes",
      "Recycling" = "Plastics"
    ),
    Category = case_when(
      # missing Category is inferred from their Type
      is.na(Category) &
        Type == "Other soil/sludges (other N)" ~
        "Hazardous wastes",
      is.na(Category) &
        Type == "Paints, resins, inks, organic sludges (F)" ~
        "Hazardous wastes",
      TRUE ~ Category
    )
  )
```

Observe new unique category

```{R}
waste_unique %>%
  select(Category) %>%
  distinct(Category) %>%
  arrange()
```

To count number of unique waste category, we get the number of rows of unique data from Category column in waste_unique table.

```{R}
# get each distinct values in Category column and count total row
number_unique_wastes_category <- waste_unique %>% 
  distinct(Category) %>%
  nrow()

number_unique_wastes_category
```

### Q1 Final Answer

Total unique "Category" values = `r number_unique_wastes_category`

## Q3. Calculate the fractions of waste tonnes of different waste sources, draw a chart to visualize the fraction numbers specific to the Category value

Observe Stream column

```{R}
waste_unique %>% 
  select(Stream) %>%
  distinct(Stream)
```

### Clean Stream column:

We observed from the Stream column: 1. "Construction and demolition waste" should be "C&I" 2. "Municipal solid waste" should be "MSW"

For consistency, all Stream values will be replace to only 3 options: C&I, C&D, MSW using recode.

```{R}
waste_unique <- waste_unique %>%
  mutate(
    Stream = recode(
      Stream,
      "Construction and demolition waste" = "C&D",
      "Municipal solid waste" = "MSW",
      
    )
  )
```

Observe new unique Stream

```{R}
waste_unique %>% 
  select(Stream) %>%
  distinct(Stream)
```

Observe Tonnes column

```{R}
waste_unique %>% 
  select(Tonnes, Description) %>%
  arrange(Tonnes)
```

### Clean Tonnes column

We observed Tonnes column contain non-sensible values: 1. Negative values

To decide on how to handle the non-sensible Tonnes value, we will start by observing how much non-sensible Tonnes value constitute in overall dataset.

```{R}
total_entries <- waste_unique %>% nrow()
total_entries

non_sensible_tonnes_entries <- waste_unique %>% filter(Tonnes < 0) %>% nrow()
non_sensible_tonnes_entries

percentage_non_sensi <- (non_sensible_tonnes_entries / total_entries) * 100

percentage_non_sensi
```

I will drop off the non-sensible Tonnes values because it constitute only less than 1% of original waste_unique dataset.

```{R}
# filter to remove negative Tonnes values
waste_tonnes_filtered <- waste_unique %>%
  mutate(Tonnes = as.numeric(Tonnes)) %>%
  filter(Tonnes >= 0)

waste_tonnes_filtered %>% 
  select(Tonnes) %>% 
  arrange(Tonnes)
```

### Calculate waste fraction

To calculate waste fraction, a new waste_fraction table is created by grouping waste_tonnes_filtered by Category and Stream. Stream_Tonnes is then obtained by summing Tonnes in each group. Category_Total is sum of Stream_Tonnes. Fraction is Stream_Tonnes / Category_Total

```{R}
waste_fraction <- waste_tonnes_filtered %>%
  group_by(Category, Stream) %>%
  summarise(Stream_Tonnes = sum(Tonnes, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  group_by(Category) %>%
  mutate(
    Category_Total = sum(Stream_Tonnes),
    Fraction = Stream_Tonnes / Category_Total
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

waste_fraction
```

### Draw chart visualizing the fraction numbers specific to the Category value

To visualise the fraction number specific to category value, I created a stacked bar plot where x-axis represent Category and y-axis represent Fraction of Tonnes, with colour of bar to distinguish each Stream.

```{R}
ggplot(
  waste_fraction, 
  aes(x = Category, y = Fraction, fill = Stream)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "fill") +
  labs(
    title = "Fraction of Waste Tonnes by Source within each Category",
    x = "Category",
    y = "Fraction of Tonnes",
    fill = "Stream"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

```

## Q4. Add the 'Year' and 'State' values from Year_State_ID.csv to Wastes.csv, compute the total waste tonnes for each year and state, and store the result in a dataset named 'temp', compute and display the statistical information (min, max, mean) of the total waste tonnes for each state in ‘temp’

Introduce a new finalised waste term for clarity

```{R}
finalised_waste <- waste_tonnes_filtered

finalised_waste
```

### Left-join year_state_id to finalised_waste.

To combine both year_state_id and finalised_waste dataset to obtain the Year and State attribute, I left joined finalised_waste to year_state_id. State is uppercased for consistency.

To calculate Tonnes_Waste_Year, Year and State are grouped in order to compute Tonnes_Waste_Year by summing Tonnes of each group.

The odd "AUSTRALIA" is filtered out since it is not a valid state.

Resulting temp table has: 1. Year 2. State 3. Total_Waste_Tonnes

```{R}
temp <- finalised_waste %>%
  left_join(year_state_id, by = c("Year_State_ID" = "ID")) %>%
  select(-Economic_Growth) %>%
  mutate(State = str_to_upper(State)) %>%
  group_by(Year, State) %>%
  summarise(Total_Waste_Tonnes = sum(Tonnes, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  filter(State != "AUSTRALIA")

temp
```

### Summary (min, q1, median, q3, max, mean) of each state

To obtain the summary, statistical metric for Total_Waste_Tonnes is obtained using summary() function. The temp_state_summary has: 1. State 2. Min 3. First_Quartile 4. Median 5. Third_Quartile 6. Max 7. Mean

```{R}
temp_state_summary <- temp %>%
  group_by(State) %>%
  summarise(
      Min = min(Total_Waste_Tonnes, na.rm = TRUE),
      First_Quartile = quantile(Total_Waste_Tonnes, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
      Median = median(Total_Waste_Tonnes, na.rm = TRUE),
      Third_Quartile = quantile(Total_Waste_Tonnes, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),
      Max = max(Total_Waste_Tonnes, na.rm = TRUE),
      Mean = mean(Total_Waste_Tonnes)
    )

temp_state_summary
```

### Q4 Final Answer
temp dataset = `r temp`
Statistical information for total waste tonnes of each state in temp = `r temp_state_summary`

## Q5. Yearly trend of total waste tonnes of food organics for each state

### Format year

To format the year from, for example: "2020-2021" to "2020", a new year_formatted table is created by left-joining finalised_waste with year_state_id. Year is extracted by concatenating the first 4 digit from original Year column.

```{R}
year_state_id
year_formatted <- finalised_waste %>%
  left_join(year_state_id, by = c("Year_State_ID" = "ID")) %>%
  mutate(State = str_to_upper(State)) %>%
  mutate(Year = as.numeric(str_extract(Year, "^\\d{4}")))

year_formatted 
```

### Filter food organics

Before analysing foor organics, a new food_organics_waste table with only data of food organics is created. The entries consist of filtered Type that equals "Food Organics". To obtain Food_Organic_Tonnes, table is grouped by Year and State, then obtained by summing each group Tonnes values.

The food_organics_waste table has: 1. Year 2. State 3. Food_Organics_Tonnes

```{R}
food_organics_waste <- year_formatted %>%
  filter(Type %in% c("Food organics")) %>%
  group_by(Year, State) %>%
  summarise(Food_Organics_Tonnes = sum(Tonnes, na.rm = TRUE))

food_organics_waste
```

### Plot food organics by year

To visualise yearly trend of food organics waste tonnes by state, a line chart is plotted with x-axis as year and y-axis as total food organics waste tonnes.

```{R}
ggplot(food_organics_waste, aes(x = Year, y = Food_Organics_Tonnes, color = State)) + 
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point() + 
  labs(
    title = "Yearly Trend of Food Organics Waste Tonnes by State",
    x = "Year",

    color = "State"

```

## Q6. Display the most recycled waste Type and the most energy-recovered waste Type with the corresponding year. Display the most increased waste Type over years

### Waste with recycling as Fate

Before analysing recycling fate waste, a new fate_recycling table with only data of recycling fate is created. The entries consist of filtered Fate that equals "Recycling".

```{R}
fate_recycling <- year_formatted %>% 
  filter(Fate %in% c("Recycling"))

fate_recycling
```

### Sum per year of each waste type with recycling as Fate

To obtain Recycled_Tonnes, fate_recycling table is grouped by Type and Year, then obtained by summing each group Tonnes values. The recycled_waste_type table has: 1. Type 2. Year 3. Recycled_Tonnes

```{R}
recycled_waste_type <- fate_recycling %>%
  group_by(Type, Year) %>%
  summarise(Recycled_Tonnes = sum(Tonnes, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  ungroup()

recycled_waste_type
```

### Most recycled waste type

To obtain the most recycled waste type, we filter entry with its Recycled_Tonnes equating to the max of the Recycled_Tonnes.

```{R}
most_recycled_waste_type <- recycled_waste_type %>%
  filter(Recycled_Tonnes == max(Recycled_Tonnes))

most_recycled_waste_type
```

### Waste with energy-recovered as Fate

Before analysing energy-recovered fate waste, a new fate_energy_recovered table with only data of energy-recovered fate is created. The entries consist of filtered Fate that equals "Energy Recovered".

```{R}
fate_energy_recovery <- year_formatted %>%
  filter(Fate %in% c("Energy recovery"))

fate_energy_recovery
```

### Sum per year of each waste type with energy-recovered as Fate

To obtain Energy_Recovered_Tonnes, fate_energy_recovered table is grouped by Type and Year, then obtained by summing each group Tonnes values. The energy_recovered_waste_type table has: 1. Type 2. Year 3. Energy_Recovered_Tonnes

```{R}
energy_recovered_waste_type <- fate_energy_recovery %>%
  group_by(Type, Year) %>%
  summarise(Energy_Recovered_Tonnes = sum(Tonnes, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  ungroup()

energy_recovered_waste_type
```

### Most energy-recovered waste type

To obtain the most energy-recovered waste type, we filter entry with its Energy_Recovered_Tonnes equating to the max of the Energy_Recovered_Tonnes

```{R}
most_energy_recovered_waste_type <- energy_recovered_waste_type %>%
  filter(Energy_Recovered_Tonnes == max(Energy_Recovered_Tonnes))

most_energy_recovered_waste_type
```

### Find first and last year data of each waste type

Create a new yearly_waste_type table with all interested years data. Change is calculated as the difference between tonnes recorded from the latest year and earliest year for each type of waste. The yearly_waste_type has: 1. Type 2. First_Year 3. Last_Year 4. First_Tonnes 5. Last_Tonnes 6. Change

```{R}
yearly_waste_type <- year_formatted %>%
  group_by(Type, Year) %>%
  summarise(
    Total_Tonnes = sum(Tonnes, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) %>%
  group_by(Type) %>%
  summarise(
    First_Year = min(Year),
    Last_Year = max(Year),
    First_Tonnes = Total_Tonnes[Year == min(Year)],
    Last_Tonnes = Total_Tonnes[Year == max(Year)],
    Change = Last_Tonnes - First_Tonnes
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

yearly_waste_type
```

### Most incremented waste type

To obtain the most incremented waste_type, filter all row to obtain Change that equates to highest changes value of the column.

```{R}
most_incremented_waste_type <- yearly_waste_type %>%
  filter(Change == max(Change))

most_incremented_waste_type  
```

### How does EIS changes in each State and economic growth across the years?
To analyse, we first create a new state_econ_score_summary table that computes the Mean_EIS, grouped by state and year. This is done by joining the 2 tables -- finalised_waste and year_state_id by Year_State_ID ad ID.
```{R}
state_econ_score_summary <- finalised_waste %>%
  # joining 2 tables
  left_join(year_state_id, by = c("Year_State_ID" = "ID")) %>%
  mutate(
    # upper State name for consistency
    State = str_to_upper(State),
    # extract first 4 digits as Year
    Year = as.numeric(str_extract(Year, "^\\d{4}"))
  ) %>%
  group_by(Year, State, Economic_Growth) %>%
  summarise(
    # mean EIS by state and year
    Mean_EIS = mean(Env_Impact_Score, na.rm = TRUE),
    n = n()
  ) %>%
  # remove "AUSTRALIA" invalid state value
  filter(State != "AUSTRALIA") %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  arrange(Year)

state_econ_score_summary

# convert state_econ_score_summary to Year, State, Metric (Mean_EIS, Economic_Growth), Value
state_econ_long <- state_econ_score_summary %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(Mean_EIS, Economic_Growth),
    names_to = "Metric",
    values_to = "Value"
  )

state_econ_long
```

Now, we can plot a line-graph containing Economic_Growth over years and Mean_EIS over year for each state. 
```{R}
ggplot(state_econ_long, aes(x = Year, y = Value, color = Metric)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point() + 
  facet_grid(Metric ~ State, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    title = "Mean EIS and Economic Growth by State over Years",
    x = "Year",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    legend.position = "none"
  )
```
